summaries.example: Imagine a recipe for checking whether a simple sentence is always true. The recipe gives exact steps, such as filling in possible answers and checking each one. A person could follow it with paper and pencil, without guessing. The Church-Turing thesis says that a Turing machine could follow the same kind of step-by-step recipe.
summaries.summary:
The Church-Turing thesis is a claim about the power of exact, step-by-step procedures. An effective method uses a finite number of precise instructions, finishes in a finite number of steps, and does not require inspiration or guessing. In the 1930s, Alonzo Church and Alan Turing each gave a precise way to describe such procedures. Turing imagined a simple machine that reads and changes symbols on a tape. Church described mathematical functions using other formal ideas. Although their approaches looked different, they turned out to agree about which functions can be calculated.

The thesis says that every effective method can be carried out by a Turing machine. This lets mathematicians replace a fuzzy question—“Can a person follow rules to get this answer?”—with a precise question about programs for a Turing machine. The entry also explains an important caution: this original thesis concerns human calculation by fixed rules. It should not automatically be confused with newer claims about all physical machines, brains, quantum computers, or the speed of computation.

The thesis helped Church and Turing show that there is no single effective decision procedure for all statements in full first-order logic. In other words, no rulebook can always examine any such statement and correctly answer whether it can be proved. Later versions of the thesis make broader claims about algorithms, physics, and machine simulation, but these are different and may have different levels of support.
key_ideas: The thesis was proposed independently by Alonzo Church and Alan Turing in the 1930s.
It connects an informal idea—following rules mechanically—with exact mathematical models.
Church used ideas such as recursive functions and lambda-definability; Turing used an abstract machine. These approaches turned out to describe the same class of functions.
The thesis is mainly about what a human rule-follower can calculate, not automatically about every possible physical machine.
Some questions, including the full decision problem for first-order logic, have no effective method that always gives the correct yes-or-no answer.
summaries.why_it_matters: The thesis gives computer science and logic a way to talk clearly about what step-by-step calculation can do. It also helps us understand that some problems are not merely difficult; they may have no universal rulebook that always solves them. The careful distinction between the original thesis and newer claims prevents us from assuming that results about Turing machines automatically settle every question about real machines or nature.

important_terms.definition: A clear set of steps that can be followed exactly, finishes after a limited number of steps, and does not require guessing or clever insight.
An imaginary machine with a tape, a reading-and-writing head, and a small set of rules. It is used to study what step-by-step calculation can do.
A task or function that can be completed by an effective method. In this entry, it often means that the answer can be worked out step by step.
A general claim that every effective method can be carried out by a Turing machine.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a recipe need exact instructions rather than just saying “use common sense”?
Could two very different-looking machines still solve exactly the same kinds of problems?
Why is showing that several models agree good evidence, but not by itself a complete proof of the thesis?
What kinds of problems might have no step-by-step method that always works?

summaries.example: Suppose a clerk is given a logical formula and a fixed truth-table procedure. The clerk writes symbols on paper, checks a finite list of cases, and eventually reports whether the formula is true in every case. This is an effective method in the technical sense: its instructions are finite and exact, it terminates, and it requires no mathematical insight during execution. Turing’s model represents the relevant activity with a finite-state machine that reads and changes symbols. If the Church-Turing thesis is accepted, asking whether the clerk has an effective method is equivalent to asking whether a Turing machine can compute the corresponding function.
summaries.summary:
The Church-Turing thesis addresses a conceptual problem at the foundations of logic and computer science: what does it mean for a function or problem to be solvable by a purely mechanical procedure? In its technical sense, an effective method has finitely many exact instructions, terminates after finitely many steps, and can be carried out by a human clerk using paper and pencil without insight, intuition, or ingenuity. This is not simply the everyday meaning of “effective” or “mechanical.”

Church and Turing independently proposed formal replacements for this informal notion in 1936. Church appealed to recursive functions and lambda-definability. Turing described a finite-state abstract machine that scans a tape, reads symbols, writes symbols, and moves according to rules. These formalisms initially appear quite different, but equivalence results showed that they determine the same class of functions. The thesis says that this shared class includes every function whose values can be obtained by an effective method. The reverse direction is comparatively straightforward for Turing machines because a machine program itself specifies a finite rule-following procedure.

Turing also offered a direct analysis of human computation. He argued that a human calculator works with finitely many symbol types, observes only finitely many squares at once, makes local changes, and passes through finitely many relevant states. A more flexible machine could simulate these features, and an ordinary Turing machine could simulate that machine. This argument depends on judgments about which features of human calculation are essential. key_ideas: Church and Turing began with an informal technical notion of effectiveness and supplied different formal analyses: recursive or lambda-definable functions in Church’s work, and Turing-machine computability in Turing’s.
The formal analyses were shown to be extensionally equivalent. This convergence is strong evidence, but equivalence alone does not prove that the shared class exactly captures every effective method.

Turing’s central argument models human rote computation using finite observations, finite states, local symbol changes, and elementary operations. A standard Turing machine can simulate the resulting process.

The status of the thesis is philosophically disputed. Some approaches treat it as provable from suitable axioms or logical results; Turing described the supporting arguments as appeals to intuition rather than ordinary mathematical proofs.

The original thesis concerns human computation by fixed rules. Claims about the limits of all machines, physical systems, brains, quantum devices, or computational efficiency are distinct modern proposals.

Church and Turing used the thesis to support the conclusion that the Entscheidungsproblem for full first-order logic is unsolvable: no effective decision procedure can always classify every formula as provable or not provable.
summaries.why_it_matters: The thesis establishes a common framework for computability theory and clarifies the difference between an unsolved problem and an unsolvable one. It also explains why the 1936 results about the Entscheidungsproblem were so important: if every effective method can be represented by a Turing machine, then proving that no Turing machine can always decide provability shows that no effective decision procedure exists. The entry’s distinctions remain important today because “Church-Turing thesis” is often extended to claims about algorithms, physical simulation, complexity, minds, or quantum systems. Those extensions are not simply the original thesis with newer examples; they are separate claims

important_terms.definition: A procedure specified by finitely many exact instructions that produces its result after finitely many steps and can be followed by a person using paper and pencil without insight or ingenuity.
An idealized computational model with a tape, a scanner, symbols, and finitely many internal states. Its behavior is determined by its current state and the symbol or symbols being examined.
A formal characterization of functions whose values can be generated by a Turing machine, or equivalently by several other formal systems developed in computability theory.
A function whose values can be obtained by an effective method; in Turing’s formulation, a function computable by a Turing machine.

The claim that every effectively calculable function is computable by a Turing machine. Its converse—that every Turing-machine computation is an effective method—is supported by the machine’s finite instructions.
The problem of finding an effective procedure that decides, for every formula in a logical calculus, whether that formula is provable.
Agreement in extension: two theories select the same class of functions, even though they may explain or represent that class in different ways.
A proposed claim that every function generated by any machine is effectively computable. The entry distinguishes this from the original Church-Turing thesis.

questions_to_think_about: Why does the agreement of Turing machines, recursive functions, lambda-definability, and other formalisms support the thesis without logically guaranteeing it?
Does Turing’s model capture every essential feature of human calculation, or could human reasoning use resources that his analysis leaves out?
Why is the claim about effective methods different from the claim that every physical machine can be simulated by a Turing machine?
If a problem has no general decision procedure, what kinds of limited or special-case procedures might still exist?
Would a mathematical proof of the thesis still depend on accepting that its axioms correctly describe effectiveness?

summaries.example: Suppose your class uses a fixed game for checking a logic puzzle. You write down every possible choice, follow the same rules for each choice, and eventually mark the puzzle “works” or “does not work.” You do not need to invent a new idea while carrying out the game. That is like an effective method. A Turing machine is an imaginary rule-following helper that reads symbols on a long tape, changes them, and moves left or right. The Church-Turing thesis says that any method of this sort can be represented by such a machine.
summaries.summary:
The Church-Turing thesis is a foundational idea about computability: the study of what can be achieved by exact rule-following procedures. An effective method, in the technical sense used by logicians, has a finite collection of precise instructions. If someone follows the instructions correctly, the method finishes after a finite number of steps. It does not ask the person to make a clever guess or use intuition while carrying out the procedure.

In the 1930s, Alonzo Church and Alan Turing tried to make this informal idea precise. Church used formal systems involving recursive functions and lambda-definability. Turing designed an abstract machine with a tape, a scanner, symbols, and a finite set of rules. The machine is not meant to imitate every detail of a modern computer. It is a model of a person doing tedious calculations on paper. Results by Church, Kleene, and Turing showed that these different approaches are extensionally equivalent: they identify the same class of functions.

The Church-Turing thesis says that every effective method belongs to this class, so it can be carried out by a Turing machine. Turing supported the claim by analyzing the essential features of human calculation: a calculator handles finitely many symbol types, sees only a limited region at a time, changes symbols locally, and proceeds through finitely many relevant states. A machine can simulate these features. Still, the argument relies on judgments about what counts as essential, so the thesis is not just a routine theorem inside mathematics.

key_ideas: The thesis began with a question about “mechanical” calculation, where that word has a special technical meaning.
Church and Turing gave different formal descriptions of computability, but their descriptions turned out to agree about which functions are computable.
Turing machines are not ordinary computers. They are mathematical models designed to capture rule-following calculation.
The thesis has evidence behind it, including many equivalent models and Turing’s analysis of human clerical work, but philosophers still discuss whether that evidence is conclusive.
The original thesis is about human calculation by fixed rules. Broader claims about all machines, brains, physics, or quantum computers should be treated separately.
Church and Turing used their ideas to argue that no general decision procedure can settle every question of provability in full first-order logic.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic shows how philosophy and mathematics work together. Before Turing and Church, “follow a mechanical procedure” was meaningful but not fully precise. Their work supplied formal models that let researchers study the idea rigorously. It also introduced a useful warning: a theorem about Turing machines does not automatically settle claims about every physical machine or every future kind of computation. Keeping these claims separate helps us reason carefully about the limits of algorithms and computers.

important_terms.definition: A method with exact instructions that can be completed in a finite number of steps without guessing, creativity, or special insight during the procedure.
A simple imaginary computer made from a tape, a symbol-reader, and rules for moving, reading, and writing. It helps mathematicians study computation.
The ability of a function or problem to be handled by a precise rule-based procedure. In the formal theory, this is represented by Turing-machine computation.
The Church-Turing claim that every effective method can be carried out by a Turing machine.
A mathematical rule that takes inputs and gives outputs. For example, a rule might take a formula as input and output 1 or 0 depending on whether it has a certain logical property.
A yes-or-no procedure for deciding whether any formula in a logical system can be proved.
The fact that different formal descriptions produce the same collection of computable functions, even though the descriptions have different meanings or structures.

questions_to_think_about: Why should a method have to finish after a finite number of steps to count as effective?
How can two different-looking models of computation agree about exactly the same functions?
Is agreement among many models enough to show that they capture every possible rule-following method?
What is the difference between “a machine can follow this algorithm” and “every possible machine can do only what a Turing machine can do”?
Why might a problem be impossible to solve by one universal procedure even if many special cases are manageable?
